newsitem.title: USA: GRAINS-US meeting to focus on value-added market.
newsitem.headline: GRAINS-US meeting to focus on value-added market.

text.p: The U.S. Feed Grains Council, in its meeting opening Monday, will get one of the best looks yet at likely U.S. production and trade as well as focusing on the budding market for value-enhanced grains.

Analysts generally foresee larger U.S. feed grain and soybean plantings this year, lured by attractive market prices. At 48.2 million acres, winter wheat sowings are down three million acres from a year ago. Half of the decline was in seven Midwestern states where corn and soybeans dominate.

More than 450 people -- double the usual turnout -- have registered for the council's "International Value Enhanced Grains Conference." Rick Tolman, the council's executive director for international operations, said the large crowd was a reflection of interest in the budding market for grain with special characteristics.
At present, only a small portion of U.S. grain fits the value-enhanced category but it can command hefty premiums.

Earlier this month, the U.S. Agricultural Marketing Service reported on cash premiums and contract pricing ranges for value-enhanced corn in Illinois. High-oil corn could fetch a 20-cent a bushel premium over No 2 yellow corn. Higher rates were possible as oil content increased above 6.5 percent.

High-starch corn could bring a 5-10 cent bonus over No 2 yellow corn, AMS reported, and waxy corn could command a 20-25 cent margin over Chicago Board of Trade futures prices. White corn was 40-50 cents a bushel above March 1998 CBOT contracts.
A Feed Grains Council report on the value-enhanced corn situation was scheduled for Monday. It prepared a similar report for last year's meeting.

"What we've found is because of a lack of information, it's hard for buyers or sellers to make a decision," Tolman said of the nascent market. "They don't know about quantities or prices." About 80 foreign buyers were registered for the conference.
A specially prepared report on the world feed grains outlook as scheduled for Tuesday morning. It would include projections on U.S. output and exports. Details were being kept confidential.

However, most analysts have been optimistic of comparatively strong grain prices in the near term and U.S. corn acreage of about 80 million acres (31.5 million hectares), which would be slightly larger than last year.

"We're anticipating large production in feed grains," said Tolman, who cautioned that he had not seen the new world grain outlook report. Large crops in Argentina and South Africa may pressure U.S. exports in the coming year, he said, but in the longer run, the United States should capture a large share of the growing demand for feed grains.
